Brain injury

A small crossover trial in mild injury reported short-term improvements in cognition, post-concussion symptoms, pain, and PTSD symptoms. A separate acute moderate-injury trial found brain-imaging differences but no PBM-specific advantage on symptom questionnaires.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A small crossover trial in mild injury reported short-term improvements in cognition, post-concussion symptoms, pain, and PTSD symptoms. A separate acute moderate-injury trial found brain-imaging differences but no PBM-specific advantage on symptom questionnaires.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact brain-injury category contains 55 unique titles: 16 human publications, 24 animal experiments, nine narrative reviews, one systematic review, one animal meta-analysis, two protocols, one perspective, and one review-or-editorial record. Human papers include case reports, series, uncontrolled studies, and two randomized clinical cohorts. Three Longo publications report different outcomes from the same moderate-injury trial; they are one cohort, not three trials. A separate 17-person sham-controlled crossover study in mild injury is a second randomized cohort.

Human and clinical evidence

In the Longo double-blind trial, 68 people with moderate traumatic brain injury were randomized to helmet-delivered near-infrared PBM or sham. The active group showed treatment-by-time differences in selected diffusion-MRI measures, and secondary analyses from the same cohort reported increased functional connectivity and magnetic-resonance spectroscopy changes. However, post-concussion symptom scores improved over time in both groups without a clear PBM-specific advantage (Longo et al. 2020 Chan et al. 2024 Ratai et al. 2025).

A separate 17-person sham-controlled crossover trial in mild injury reported better visual working memory and verbal learning after PBM, along with fewer physical post-concussion symptoms, less pain, improved sleep, and lower PTSD symptoms (Lee et al. 2025). In a nine-person chronic mild-injury pilot, two participants improved on objective neuropsychological testing; some participants reported better cognition or fewer symptoms, but most did not improve on testing (Karr et al. 2024).

Animal evidence

The 24 animal publications include 12 mouse, 11 rat, and one fruit-fly study. Across models, researchers have measured motor and cognitive performance, lesion size, inflammation, and tissue repair. A systematic review with animal meta-analysis found pooled results favoring PBM for neurological severity scores and lesion size in acute injury models (Stevens et al. 2022). These preclinical outcomes support the direction of the experimental findings but do not resolve which patient group or clinical schedule benefits.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate in-vitro or ex-vivo paper is classified in the exact brain-injury category. Cellular mechanisms were generally measured within animal experiments or discussed in reviews.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The clinical studies use red or near-infrared light delivered through helmets or localized transcranial devices. The Longo trial used 810 nm near-infrared LED light, with three 20-minute sessions begun during the first 72 hours; the reported scalp fluence was 43 J/cm², with a much lower estimated dose at the cortex. Other records use 633 nm red visible light, 870 nm near-infrared light, or 1064 nm near-infrared laser. The studies differ in injury severity, chronicity, device, and schedule, and do not establish a single optimal protocol.

Interpretation

The small crossover study in mild injury reported improvements across several short-term outcomes, while the acute moderate-injury trial found imaging responses without a corresponding symptom advantage over sham. The results therefore differ by population and outcome rather than forming one uniform clinical effect. The next useful evidence is a larger trial that measures everyday function and symptom durability while separating mild from moderate injury.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term cognition and symptoms in mild traumatic brain injury Low for symptoms after acute moderate traumatic brain injury
Publications and records55 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One small sham-controlled crossover trial reported short-term cognitive and symptom improvements in mild injury, while a separate pilot found self-reported gains in some participants but little objective test change. In acute moderate injury, the randomized trial found imaging responses without a clear symptom advantage over sham. Larger controlled studies should test functional recovery and durability separately by injury severity and timing.
